topic_tag: probability distribution with unknown probabilities and a given expected value
subskill: the probabilities sum to 1 (p + q = 0.65) and the expected value equation gives p + 3q = 2.13 − 0.40 − 0.20 = 1.53; solve the system for p
prompt: A random variable X takes only the values 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4. The probabilities are P(X = 0) = 0.10, P(X = 1) = p, P(X = 2) = 0.20, P(X = 3) = q, and P(X = 4) = 0.05, where p and q are constants. The expected value of X is 2.13. What is the value of p ?
explanation: The probabilities sum to 1, so p + q = 1 − 0.10 − 0.20 − 0.05 = 0.65. The expected value is 0(0.10) + 1p + 2(0.20) + 3q + 4(0.05) = 2.13, so p + 3q = 2.13 − 0.40 − 0.20 = 1.53. Subtracting, 2q = 0.88, so q = 0.44 and p = 0.21. The option "0.44" is q, the other unknown. The option "0.36" leaves P(X = 0) out of the sum, using p + q = 0.75. The option "0.26" counts P(X = 0) as contributing 0.10 to the expected value, as if X were 1 there.

distractor_kind.0.44: error path: reports q instead of p. (a) limiting case: 0 < p < 0.65 since p + q = 0.65; 0.44 inside. (b) neighbouring setup: q is the other unknown of the same system, an intermediate value, and sits strictly inside (0, 0.65), not on an end. (c) cheapest estimate: (0, 0.65); strictly inside. (d) real: wrong variable.
distractor_kind.0.36: error path: omits P(X = 0) from the total. (a) inside (0, 0.65). (b) no. (c) inside. (d) real: dropped term in the sum to 1.
distractor_kind.0.26: error path: weights the X = 0 row by 1 in the mean. (a) inside. (b) no. (c) inside. (d) real: value-probability confusion.

arith_class_check: No. All four are 2-decimal probabilities with distinct last digits; the stem implies only 0 < p < 0.65, which all four satisfy.
one_sided_check: Key smallest. No: reporting q, dropping P(X = 0) from the total and mis-weighting the X = 0 row are three different errors; a student cannot read from the stem that each produces a larger value, and all lie inside (0, 0.65).
interior_parity_check: interior options by value 0.26 and 0.36; both 2-decimal values below 1 with nonzero last digit, complexity 4 and 4; neither is rounder.

topic_tag: expected number of successes when drawing without replacement
subskill: each of the 3 draws is red with probability 5/12 (by symmetry), so the expected number of red marbles is 3(5/12) = 1.25, even though the draws are not independent
prompt: A bag contains 5 red marbles and 7 blue marbles. Three marbles are drawn at random, one at a time, without replacement. To the nearest hundredth, what is the expected number of red marbles drawn?
explanation: P(0 red) = C(7,3)/C(12,3) = 35/220, P(1) = 5·21/220 = 105/220, P(2) = 10·7/220 = 70/220, P(3) = 10/220. The expected number is (105 + 140 + 30)/220 = 275/220 = 1.25. (Equivalently, each draw is red with probability 5/12, so the expected count is 3 · 5/12.) The option "1.09" assumes every draw happens after one red marble has been removed, 3 · 4/11. The option "1.36" removes one marble from the total but not from the reds, 3 · 5/11. The option "2.14" uses the ratio of red to blue, 3 · 5/7, as the chance of red.
solve: const C=(n,k)=>{let r=1;for(let i=0;i<k;i++) r=r*(n-i)/(i+1);return r;}; let e=0; for(let k=0;k<=3;k++) e+=k*C(5,k)*C(7,3-k)/C(12,3); return e.toFixed(2);
quantity_asked: the expected number of red marbles among 3 drawn without replacement from 5 red and 7 blue.

distractor_kind.1.09: error path: 3 x 4/11. (a) limiting case: 0 <= v <= 3; inside. (b) neighbouring setup: not an extreme. (c) cheapest estimate: the expected count is 3 x (5/12) by symmetry, which is the item itself; no cheaper bracket than [0, 3]; inside. (d) real: decremented both counts for every draw.
distractor_kind.1.36: error path: 3 x 5/11. (a) inside [0, 3]. (b) no. (c) inside. (d) real: decremented only the total.
distractor_kind.2.14: error path: odds 5:7 used as probability. (a) inside [0, 3]. (b) no. (c) inside. (d) real: ratio for probability.

arith_class_check: No. The stem does not imply a terminating decimal; options are 2-decimal values (.36, .14, .25, .09) and the key happening to terminate is not stem-readable.
interior_parity_check: interior options by value 1.25 and 1.36; both 2-decimal numbers with one integer digit, complexity 5 and 5; neither is rounder by the display rule.

topic_tag: probability by counting: selection avoiding pairs
subskill: count 4-person selections with no married pair: choose 4 of the 5 couples, then 1 spouse from each, C(5,4)·2^4 = 80, out of C(10,4) = 210 (or multiply 8/9 · 6/8 · 4/7 pick by pick)
prompt: A group of 10 people consists of 5 married couples. Four of the 10 people are chosen at random to form a committee, with every group of 4 equally likely to be chosen. To the nearest hundredth, what is the probability that no two of the people chosen are married to each other?
explanation: There are C(10,4) = 210 equally likely committees. A committee with no married pair uses 4 different couples, C(5,4) = 5 ways, and one spouse from each of those couples, 2⁴ = 16 ways: 80 committees. The probability is 80/210 ≈ 0.38. (Pick by pick: after the first person, the second must avoid 1 of the 9 remaining people, the third 2 of 8, the fourth 3 of 7: (8/9)(6/8)(4/7) = 80/210.) The option "0.02" chooses the 4 couples but forgets that either spouse can be chosen from each, 5/210. The option "0.48" lets the fourth person avoid only 2 people, (8/9)(6/8)(5/7). The option "0.56" lets the third person avoid only 1 person and the fourth only 2, (8/9)(7/8)(5/7).
solve: const C=(n,k)=>{let r=1;for(let i=0;i<k;i++) r=r*(n-i)/(i+1);return r;}; return (C(5,4)*16/C(10,4)).toFixed(2);

distractor_solve.0.02: const C=(n,k)=>{let r=1;for(let i=0;i<k;i++) r=r*(n-i)/(i+1);return r;}; return (C(5,4)/C(10,4)).toFixed(2);

quantity_asked: the fraction of the 210 four-person committees that contain no married couple.

distractor_kind.0.02: error path: C(5,4)/C(10,4), spouse choice 2^4 dropped. (a) limiting case: 0 < v and v <= P(first three chosen include no couple) = (8/9)(6/8) = 2/3; 0.02 inside. (b) neighbouring setup: not an extreme. (c) cheapest estimate: (0, 2/3); strictly inside. (d) real: forgot the factor for choosing a spouse.
distractor_kind.0.48: error path: fourth pick excludes 2 people instead of 3. (a) inside (0, 2/3). (b) no. (c) inside. (d) real: lost track of excluded spouses.
distractor_kind.0.56: error path: third pick excludes 1 and fourth excludes 2. (a) inside (0, 2/3). (b) no. (c) inside. (d) real: excluded only the most recent spouse at each step.

mechanism: choose couples then one spouse each
arith_class_check: No. All options are 2-decimal probabilities with distinct last digits; the stem implies a fraction over 210 but nothing that isolates the key.
interior_parity_check: interior options by value 0.38 and 0.48; both 2-decimal values below 1 with nonzero last digit, complexity 4 and 4; neither is rounder.

topic_tag: probability by counting with the triangle inequality
subskill: three lengths a <= b <= c form a triangle exactly when a + b > c (strictly); count such triples among the C(7,3) = 35 equally likely sets
prompt: Seven sticks have lengths 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 9, and 10 centimeters. Three of the sticks are chosen at random, with every set of 3 sticks equally likely to be chosen. To the nearest hundredth, what is the probability that the 3 sticks chosen can be placed end to end to form a triangle?
explanation: There are C(7,3) = 35 equally likely sets. Listing each set with a < b < c and checking a + b > c gives 16 sets that form a triangle: (2,3,4), (2,4,5), (2,8,9), (2,9,10), (3,4,5), (3,8,9), (3,8,10), (3,9,10), (4,5,8), (4,8,9), (4,8,10), (4,9,10), (5,8,9), (5,8,10), (5,9,10), (8,9,10). The probability is 16/35 ≈ 0.46. The option "0.57" also counts the 4 sets with a + b = c, such as (2,3,5) and (4,5,9), which only lie flat. The option "0.76" divides by C(7,2) = 21 instead of C(7,3). The option "0.84" gives the odds 16 : 19 instead of the probability.
solve: const L=[2,3,4,5,8,9,10]; let ok=0,n=0; for(let i=0;i<7;i++)for(let j=i+1;j<7;j++)for(let k=j+1;k<7;k++){n++; if(L[i]+L[j]>L[k]) ok++;} return (ok/n).toFixed(2);

distractor_solve.0.57: const L=[2,3,4,5,8,9,10]; let ok=0,n=0; for(let i=0;i<7;i++)for(let j=i+1;j<7;j++)for(let k=j+1;k<7;k++){n++; if(L[i]+L[j]>=L[k]) ok++;} return (ok/n).toFixed(2);
distractor_solve.0.76: const L=[2,3,4,5,8,9,10]; let ok=0; for(let i=0;i<7;i++)for(let j=i+1;j<7;j++)for(let k=j+1;k<7;k++){ if(L[i]+L[j]>L[k]) ok++;} return (ok/21).toFixed(2);
distractor_solve.0.84: const L=[2,3,4,5,8,9,10]; let ok=0,n=0; for(let i=0;i<7;i++)for(let j=i+1;j<7;j++)for(let k=j+1;k<7;k++){n++; if(L[i]+L[j]>L[k]) ok++;} return (ok/(n-ok)).toFixed(2);

quantity_asked: the fraction of the 35 three-stick sets that satisfy the strict triangle inequality.

distractor_kind.0.57: error path: counts degenerate sets (a + b = c) as triangles. (a) limiting case: 0 < v < 1; inside. (b) neighbouring setup: the non-strict-inequality version; not an extreme. (c) cheapest estimate: no bracket short of enumerating; inside. (d) real.
distractor_kind.0.76: error path: denominator C(7,2) = 21. (a) inside (0, 1). (b) no. (c) inside. (d) real: wrong combination count.
distractor_kind.0.84: error path: favourable : unfavourable = 16/19. (a) inside (0, 1). (b) no. (c) inside. (d) real: odds for probability.

arith_class_check: No. Options are 2-decimal values (.46, .84, .57, .76); the stem implies a fraction over 35 but 0.46 and 0.57 are both consistent with that, so the class does not isolate the key.
one_sided_check: Key smallest. No: counting flat triples, using C(7,2) and reporting odds are three different errors; the stem gives no readable reason that every natural mistake raises the value.
interior_parity_check: interior options by value 0.57 and 0.76; both 2-decimal values below 1 with nonzero last digit, complexity 4 and 4; neither is rounder.

topic_tag: conditional probability across two dependent events
subskill: rain on exactly one day is the union of (rain Saturday, dry Sunday) and (dry Saturday, rain Sunday); multiply along each branch with the matching conditional probability and add
prompt: The probability that it rains on Saturday is 0.40. If it rains on Saturday, the probability that it rains on Sunday is 0.65. If it does not rain on Saturday, the probability that it rains on Sunday is 0.30. What is the probability that it rains on exactly one of the two days?
explanation: Rain on Saturday only: 0.40 × (1 − 0.65) = 0.14. Rain on Sunday only: (1 − 0.40) × 0.30 = 0.18. The probability of rain on exactly one day is 0.14 + 0.18 = 0.32. The option "0.26" is the probability of rain on both days, 0.40 × 0.65. The option "0.44" is the probability of rain on Sunday, 0.26 + 0.18. The option "0.67" pairs each Saturday outcome with the wrong conditional probability, 0.40 × 0.70 + 0.60 × 0.65.
quantity_asked: P(rain on Saturday and not Sunday) + P(no rain Saturday and rain Sunday).

distractor_kind.0.26: error path: P(both days). (a) limiting case: 0 < v < 1; inside. (b) neighbouring setup: the "both days" event is disjoint from "exactly one", so it bounds nothing; inside. (c) cheapest estimate: no bracket short of the two branch products; inside. (d) real: wrong event.
distractor_kind.0.44: error path: P(rain on Sunday). (a) inside (0, 1). (b) the marginal for Sunday overlaps "exactly one" but neither contains the other; not a bound. (c) inside. (d) real: wrong event.
distractor_kind.0.67: error path: conditionals attached to the wrong Saturday branch. (a) inside. (b) no. (c) inside. (d) real: swapped conditionals.

mechanism: rain on exactly one of two days
arith_class_check: No. All options are 2-decimal probabilities; last digits 4, 6, 7, 2 are all different; nothing in the stem implies a class.
interior_parity_check: interior options by value 0.32 and 0.44; both 2-decimal values below 1 with nonzero last digit, complexity 4 and 4; neither is rounder.
